Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: XXXIII. Ad solvendam hanc difficultatem observandum est, apud Protestantes gratiam regenerationis & justificationis modo latius, modo strictius sumi. Ex Protestantium sensu, justificatio stricte & praecise accepta, non est aliud quam hominis peccatoris absolutio, propter Christi satisfactionem ipsi donatam atque imputatam, & sic concipitur ut beneficium distinctum a fide, per quam simus illius participes, & quae ideo fides justificans vocatur. Sub gratia vero justificationis, si latius sumatur, includitur ipsa fides per quam justificamur. Hoc sensu sumunt Protestantes justificationem, quum negant ulla opera vere bona illam antecedere. Idem enim cum ipsis est antecedere justificationem quod antecedere fidem justificantem. Nihilque eatenus justificationem praecedit, quod non fidem etiam praecedat. Adeoque quum dicunt omnia quae fiunt ante justificationem, non esse bona opera, sed peccata, non aliud sibi volunt, quam ante fidem nullum bonum opus in homine existere posse, sed omnia infidelium opera esse peccata.
english: Thesis XXXIII. To solve this difficulty we must note that the Protestants use 'the grace of regeneration and justification' sometimes in a wider and sometimes in a stricter sense. In their usage, justification taken strictly and precisely is nothing but the absolution of a sinner for the sake of Christ's satisfaction, which is given and imputed to him. Understood in this way it is a benefit distinct from faith, the faith by which we share in it and which is therefore called justifying faith.

Taken more widely, though, the grace of justification includes the very faith by which we are justified. This is the sense the Protestants have in mind when they deny that any truly good works precede justification. For them, to come before justification is the same as to come before justifying faith, and nothing precedes justification that does not also precede faith.

So when they say that everything done before justification is sin and not a good work, they mean only that no good work can exist in a man before faith, and that all the works of unbelievers are sins.

source_text: XXXIV. Id videre est apud Calvinum atque Kemnitium, ubi censura sua notant Canonem jam dictum Synodi Tridentinae. Kemnitius enim Canonem illum damnans, supponit per eum anathema dici illis qui negant infideles, per sua opera se disponere ad gratiam. Nam, inquit, Canone septimo anathema dicunt illis, qui negant infideles per sua opera se disponere ad gratiam. In prima parte Examinis pagina 157. col. a. In praecedentibus vero justificationem sensu strictiori sumens, fatetur poenitentiam, fidem, contritionem, & propositum in peccato non pergendi, esse secundum scripturam praeparationes quasdam ad justificationem. Vult enim Deus, inquit, a notitia & assensu verbi sui nos ordiri. Et ante justificationem oportet praecedere contritionem, hoc est, seriam agnitionem peccatorum, pavores conscientiae agnoscentis iram Dei adversus nostra peccata, & dolentis propter peccatum, in qua contritione non retinetur, sed abjicitur propositum perseverandi & pergendi in sceleribus. Ad hoc vero necesse est accedere fidem, quae agnitione & fiducia misericordiae Dei promissae, propter filium Mediatorem, rursus erigat & consoletur animum, ne oppressi desperatione ruamus in aeternum exitium: sed fides accedat ad Deum, quaerat, desideret, petat, apprehendat & accipiat remissionem peccatorum. Pag. 155.
english: Thesis XXXIV. This can be seen in Calvin and Chemnitz, where they censure the canon of the Council of Trent already mentioned. Chemnitz, condemning that canon, takes it to pronounce anathema on those who deny that unbelievers dispose themselves for grace by their works: 'In the seventh canon,' he says, 'they pronounce anathema on those who deny that unbelievers dispose themselves for grace by their works' (Examination, part 1, page 157, column a).

But earlier in the same work, taking justification in the stricter sense, he admits that penitence, faith, contrition and the resolve not to go on in sin are, according to Scripture, certain preparations for justification. 'God wills,' he says, 'that we begin from knowledge of his word and assent to it. And contrition must come before justification: that is, a serious acknowledgement of our sins, the terrors of a conscience that recognises God's wrath against our sins and grieves over sin. In this contrition the resolve to persist and go on in wickedness is not kept but thrown away.

Faith must be added to this, so that by knowing and trusting the mercy God has promised for the sake of his Son the Mediator it may raise up and comfort the mind again, and we may not be crushed by despair and rush into eternal ruin. Faith must rather come to God, seek, desire, ask for, lay hold of and receive the forgiveness of sins' (page 155).

source_text: XXXV. Et similiter Calvinus eundem illum Canonem Concilii Tridentini refutans non aliis utitur argumentis, quam quae probant sine fide nihil boni fieri posse. Ut quod Deus non moratur externas larvas, sed fidem cordis inspicit. Quod non nisi fide purificantur corda. Quod quicquid agant infideles, facta sua ad Deum non referunt. Quod denique, juxta Augustinum, si quis bonus fructus in homine laudatur, in fide quaerenda est radix. Et Religio nostra justos ab injustis, non operum, sed ipsa fidei lege discernit, sine qua quae videntur bona opera, in peccata vertuntur. In antidoto ad septimum Canonem Sessionis sextae. Unde patet Calvino eo loci idem esse aliquid facere ante justificationem, quod facere ante fidem & in infidelitate. Nec illum aliud velle quam quod omnia opera ante fidem non bona, sed mala sint. Cum quo optime constat justificationem pro remissione peccatorum acceptam, seu pro peccatoris absolutione, praevios habere quosdam non solum fidei actus, sed timoris, spei & dilectionis, ac propositi novae vitae, qui boni sint & Deo grati.
english: Thesis XXXV. Calvin likewise, refuting the same canon of the Council of Trent, uses no arguments except those that prove nothing good can be done without faith. God does not care for outward masks but looks at the faith of the heart; hearts are purified only by faith; whatever unbelievers do, they do not refer their deeds to God; and finally, as Augustine says, if any good fruit in a man is praised, its root must be looked for in faith.

And 'our religion distinguishes the just from the unjust not by the law of works but by the law of faith itself, without which what look like good works are turned into sins' (Antidote, on canon 7 of the sixth session). It is plain, then, that for Calvin in this place doing something before justification is the same as doing it before faith and in unbelief, and that he means only that all works before faith are bad and not good.

This fits very well with the view that justification, taken as the forgiveness of sins or the sinner's absolution, is preceded by certain acts, not only of faith but also of fear, hope and love, and by the resolve to live a new life, which are good and pleasing to God.

source_text: XXXVI. Eodem modo regeneratio seu sanctificatio aliquando stricte accipitur, pro habituali quadam hominis immutatione per habitus justitiae & sanctitatis infusos, quandoque vero latius pro omnibus illis gratiae divinae in nobis effectis, quibus a statu peccati in statum justitiae & filiorum Dei transferimur. Et sic gratia regenerationis, sive sanctificationis complectitur initium, progressum & complementum, efficacis illius gratiae per quam Deus peccati Dominium in nobis abolet, & nos efficit justitiae servos, sive ut loquitur scriptura, facit ut veterem hominem exuamus, & induamus novum, qui secundum Deum creatus est, in justitia & sanctitate veritatis, Quod dicit Amesius regenerationem aliquando sumi pro tota serie auxiliorum, quibus ad eam movemur. Disput. Theologica de praeparatione peccatoris ad conversionem. Thesi 11.
english: Thesis XXXVI. In the same way regeneration, or sanctification, is sometimes taken strictly, for a habitual change in a man through infused habits of righteousness and holiness. Sometimes it is taken more widely, for all the effects of divine grace in us by which we are brought from the state of sin into the state of righteousness and of the children of God.

Taken so, the grace of regeneration or sanctification includes the beginning, the progress and the completion of the efficacious grace by which God abolishes the dominion of sin in us and makes us servants of righteousness. In Scripture's words, it makes us put off the old man and put on the new, created after God in righteousness and true holiness. This is what Ames means when he says that regeneration is sometimes taken for the whole series of helps by which we are moved toward it (Theological disputation on the preparation of the sinner for conversion, thesis 11).

source_text: XXXVII. Regeneratio sumpta priori illo & strictiori sensu, praevios habet plures actus fidei, spei, timoris, doloris de peccato, dilectionis quoque, & implorationis auxilii divini, qui proculdubio opera bona sunt & Deo accepta, quibusque homo ex Dei instituto praeparatur ad accipiendum donum spiritus sanctificantis atque regenerantis. Adeoque gratia regenerationis stricto illo sensu sumptae ad illa facienda necessaria non est. Sed sine gratia regenerationis, acceptae posteriori & latiori sensu, nemo quicquam boni operari potest. Nam impossibile est hominem bene agere, priusquam Deus incipiat per gratiam suam in eo operari, ut eum exolvat a peccati vinculis, & in filiorum Dei libertatem asserat. Cujus gratiae prima initia ad regenerationem latius sumptam, ut jam diximus, revocantur.
english: Thesis XXXVII. Regeneration taken in the first, stricter sense is preceded by many acts of faith, hope, fear, sorrow for sin, love too, and prayer for God's help. These are undoubtedly good works, acceptable to God, by which a man is prepared, as God has ordained, to receive the gift of the sanctifying and regenerating Spirit. So the grace of regeneration in that strict sense is not needed for doing them.

But without the grace of regeneration taken in the second and wider sense, no one can do anything good. A man cannot possibly act well before God begins to work in him by his grace, to free him from the chains of sin and set him in the liberty of God's children. As already said, the first beginnings of that grace belong to regeneration taken more widely.

source_text: XXXVIII. Etsi vero gratia prorsus necessaria sit, ad hoc ut homo corruptus possit aliquod bonum opus facere, nec sine gratia valeat quicquam operari bene & divinae legi conformiter: id tamen non obstat, ex Protestantium sensu, quominus in eo statu homo, dum male agit, sive committendo ea quae lex prohibet, sive omittendo ea quae praecipit, id libere faciat, & vim nativam liberi sui arbitrii exerat.
english: Thesis XXXVIII. Grace is wholly necessary if corrupt man is to do any good work, and without grace he can do nothing well and in conformity with God's law.

Yet in the Protestants' view this does not prevent man in that state from acting freely when he does evil, whether by committing what the law forbids or omitting what it commands; in doing so he exercises the native power of his free choice.

source_text: XXXIX. Quamvis enim absente gratia, Homo sit peccati servus, ut scriptura loquitur, & quicquid agat non possit nisi peccare: ista tamen male agendi necessitas naturalem arbitrii ejus libertatem non tollit. Libertas enim illa quae essentialis est omni agenti intellectu & voluntate praedito, non consistit in eo ut quis indifferens sit ad bene vel male agendum, & parem ad utrumque facultatem habeat. Alioqui nec daemones in inferno, nec Angeli in coelo libere operarentur, cum illi quidem ad male agendum, hi vero contra ad bene agendum sint determinati. Verum in eo sita est ista naturalis arbitrii libertas, ut quis agat non coactus, nec etiam bruto naturae impulsu, sed praevio mentis judicio & deliberatione eligat quod ipsi lubet & videtur. Adeoque libertas illa opponitur coactioni, & naturali, seu brutae determinationi, minime vero servituti peccati, quae non obstat quominus homo, dum peccat, deliberate agat, & ex rationis propriae dictamine, absque ulla coactione, & naturali seu bruta determinatione.
english: Thesis XXXIX. Without grace man is the servant of sin, as Scripture says, and whatever he does he cannot help sinning. Yet this necessity of doing evil does not take away the natural freedom of his choice. The freedom that belongs essentially to every agent with intellect and will does not consist in being indifferent between acting well and acting badly, with an equal power for either. Otherwise neither the demons in hell nor the angels in heaven would act freely, since the demons are fixed on doing evil and the angels, conversely, on doing good.

That natural freedom of choice consists rather in acting without compulsion and without any brute impulse of nature, choosing what one pleases and thinks fit after a prior judgement and deliberation of the mind. So this freedom is opposed to coercion and to natural or brute determination, but not at all to the bondage of sin. That bondage does not stop a man, when he sins, from acting deliberately and at the dictate of his own reason, without any coercion and without natural or brute determination.

source_text: XL. Adde quod homo in statu peccati sibi relictus, in genere quidem ad male agendum determinatus est, non tamen ad singulas malas actiones est determinatus, sed potest ab hac vel illa abstinere: sicut homo carcere conclusus potest per carcerem libere discurrere. Qua similitudine ad hanc rem illustrandam utitur Gulielmus Perkinsus, Nam, inquit, esse quasdam res, quae necessario & libere simul fiant, exemplo demonstrabo. Sit aliquis in carcerem detrusus, cui necessario ibi sit manendum, quique non possit exire quo velit. Is tamen talis movere se potest, ac libere deambulare intra ipsum carcerem. Similiter se res habet cum voluntate humana, quae licet peccati vinculis constricta, naturaliter aliud non faciat quam ut peccet, atque ita peccet necessario: tamen eadem peccat propria ac libera voluntate. In Catholico Reformato, Controversia prima de libero arbitrio Conclusione quarta.
english: Thesis XL. Add that man in the state of sin, left to himself, is indeed determined to evil in general, but not to each particular evil action: he can abstain from this one or that one, just as a man locked in prison can walk about freely inside it. William Perkins uses this comparison to illustrate the point.

'I will show by an example,' he says, 'that some things are done necessarily and freely at the same time. Suppose a man has been thrown into prison, so that he must stay there and cannot leave for wherever he wants. He can still move about and walk freely within the prison. It is the same with the human will. Bound by the chains of sin, it naturally does nothing but sin, and so sins necessarily; yet it sins of its own free will' (The Reformed Catholic, first controversy, On free will, fourth conclusion).

source_text: XLI. Similiter gratiae cum adest praesentia atque efficacia, ex Protestantium mente, nihil omnino praejudicat humanae libertati. Neque minus liberae sunt actiones quae gratia movente & auxiliante fiunt, quam si absque gratia fieri supponantur. Nec enim gratia vim ullam humanae voluntati affert, sed eam movet liberae facultati congruenter, nimirum praeeunte & interveniente deliberato mentis judicio, & sic ut a voluntate non tollat aliter agendi potestatem. Adeoque bona quaelibet opera, ita sunt effecta gratiae divinae, ut sint etiam actus liberi arbitrii a gratia liberati, & agentis non ex propriis viribus, sed ex illis quas ipsi gratia suppeditavit.
english: Thesis XLI. Likewise, in the Protestants' mind, the presence and efficacy of grace, when it is at work, does no harm at all to human freedom. Actions done with grace moving and helping are no less free than they would be if they were supposed done without grace.

Grace does no violence to the human will; it moves it in a way suited to a free faculty, with a deliberate judgement of the mind going before and accompanying the act, and without taking from the will the power to act otherwise. So all good works are effects of divine grace in such a way that they are also acts of a free choice set free by grace, which acts not by its own powers but by those grace has supplied.

source_text: XLII. Neque sic in hac vita per gratiam liberatur hominis arbitrium, quin semper, ut bene, sic male agere possit: sicut ultro Paraeus contra Bellarminum disputans agnoscit. Quis Christianus, inquit, unquam dubitavit hominem donatum gratia arbitrium habere liberatum & liberum ad bonum eligendum, praestandum ex vi gratiae: ad malum quoque eligendum, faciendum ex imbecillitate naturae, quae a gratia nec regeneratur, nec regitur perfecte in hac vita: unde renati libertate voluntatis, tam ad bene quam ad male operandum, in hac vita utuntur? Nulla igitur haec quaestio esse potest, utrum posito gratiae auxilio homo sit vere liberi arbitrii? In librum V. Bellarmini de Gratia & libero arbitrio, capite XIII. Quibus conformia sunt quae repetit author ille, ejusdem libri capite XXVIII. In statu gratiae sic libere eligit bonum voluntas renovata, ut dum ad id eligendum efficaciter movetur a gratia, possit quidem contrarium eligere per defectum naturae, nolit vero per efficaciam gratiae.
english: Thesis XLII. Nor is man's choice so freed by grace in this life that he cannot always act badly as well as well, as Pareus, disputing against Bellarmine, freely admits. 'What Christian,' he says, 'ever doubted that a man endowed with grace has a choice that is set free and free to choose good and do it by the power of grace, and also to choose evil and do it out of the weakness of nature, which grace neither regenerates nor governs perfectly in this life? Hence the reborn use their freedom of will in this life both to do well and to do badly.

So there can be no question whether a man, given the help of grace, truly has free choice' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 13). The same author repeats this in chapter 28 of that book: 'In the state of grace the renewed will chooses good freely, in such a way that while it is effectively moved by grace to choose it, it can indeed choose the opposite through the defect of nature, but does not will to, because of the efficacy of grace.'

source_text: XLIII. Quod si quis quaerat An homo in statu naturae lapsae, sine gratia, sit liber ad bonum morale eligendum, & praecepta Dei servanda? ad hoc negative respondent Protestantes: adeoque eorum plurimi negant post peccatum in homine mansisse liberum arbitrium respectu boni moralis. Non aliud tamen per hoc sibi volunt, quam hominem per suum lapsum factum esse servum & captivum peccati, ejusque arbitrium privatum esse ea libertate quae servituti peccati opponitur: licet in eo manserit libertas illa quae essentialis est agenti intellectuali, & a qua hominis arbitrium absolute consideratum liberum denominatur.
english: Thesis XLIII. If someone asks whether man in the state of fallen nature is free, without grace, to choose moral good and keep God's commandments, the Protestants answer no. So most of them deny that free choice remained in man after sin with regard to moral good.

All they mean by this, though, is that by his fall man became the slave and captive of sin, and his choice lost the freedom that is opposed to the bondage of sin. The freedom essential to an intellectual agent still remained in him, the freedom from which man's choice, considered absolutely, is called free.

source_text: XLIV. Ad quaestionem ergo a Bellarmino propositam, sit ne homo in statu naturae lapsae liberi arbitrii in bono morali eligendo & malo evitando, sive, quod idem est, in praeceptis morum observandis, aut praevaricandis? Respondent per distinctionem, videlicet, in eo statu hominem ante gratiam liberi arbitrii esse in praeceptis morum violandis atque praevaricandis. Posita vero gratia, illum arbitrii sui libertate uti posse tam ad praecepta morum observanda, quam ad illa transgredienda. Sine gratia autem illum non esse arbitrii liberi ad eadem praecepta servanda; quoniam absente gratia in bono nihil potest, non ex defectu Physicae alicujus facultatis; semper enim praeditus est mente & voluntate, quae essentiali quadam libertate nunquam spoliantur, & praeter quas nulla naturalis facultas requiritur ad bonum faciendum: sed quia voluntas ejus in malo obfirmata est, donec per gratiam a Deo liberetur, & exolvatur servitute peccati, quae cum priori illa libertate consistere potest.
english: Thesis XLIV. To the question Bellarmine poses, then, whether man in the state of fallen nature has free choice in choosing moral good and avoiding evil, or, which is the same thing, in keeping or breaking the moral precepts, they answer with a distinction. In that state, before grace, man has free choice in violating and breaking the moral precepts. Once grace is given, he can use the freedom of his choice both to keep them and to break them.

Without grace, however, he does not have free choice to keep those precepts. Without grace he can do nothing good, not through the lack of some physical faculty, for he always has a mind and a will, which are never stripped of their essential freedom, and no other natural faculty is needed for doing good. The reason is that his will is set fast in evil until God frees it by grace and releases it from the bondage of sin, a bondage that can coexist with the freedom just described.

source_text: XLV. Itaque queruntur sibi per calumniam a Bellarmino & aliis imputari, quod sive cum gratia, sive ante gratiam, doceant hominem in moralibus nunquam liberi arbitrii esse. Quis, inquit Paraeus, hominem per nos nunquam habere liberum arbitrium, dixerit citra insignem calumniam? In statu peccati arbitrium habet liberum tantum ad malum, quia captivum ad bonum: In statu gratiae liberum ad utrumque. An nunquam ergo habet liberum arbitrium? In lib. V. Bellar. de gratia & libero arbitrio cap. 28.
english: Thesis XLV. So they complain that Bellarmine and others slander them by charging that they teach that man never has free choice in moral matters, whether with grace or before it.

'Who could say without flagrant slander,' asks Pareus, 'that on our view man never has free choice? In the state of sin choice is free only for evil, because it is captive as regards good; in the state of grace it is free for both. Does it never have free choice, then?' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 28).

source_text: XLVI. Porro ex iis quae tum in hac, tum in praecedenti disputatione latius exposita sunt, patet Scholam Romanam cum Protestantibus in eo consentire, quod praecepta legis moralis, sine gratia non possint ab homine lapso eo modo servari, quo sunt ad beatitudinem coelestem ordinata, & sic ut eorum observatio ad vitam aeternam homini jus acquirat, ac sempiternam ejus salutem promoveat. Vicissim vero Protestantes agnoscere cum Schola Romana, hominem lapsum, sine gratia Christi, posse servare quaedam legis moralis praecepta, saltem quoad opus externum, sive absolute, & quoad materiam vel effectionem operis ipsius, ut loquuntur Protestantes. Quod Schola Romana dicit secundum operis substantiam. Haec enim eodem redeunt, quamvis Protestantes nonnulli posteriorem istum loquendi modum improbent: quia substantia rei materiam & formam comprehendit. Hic autem agitur non de operis moralis forma, quae a fine & principio pendet, sed de materia tantum.
english: Thesis XLVI. From what has been set out at length both in this disputation and in the one before it, it is plain that the Roman School agrees with the Protestants on one point: fallen man cannot without grace keep the precepts of the moral law in the way in which they are ordered to heavenly happiness, so that keeping them gains him a right to eternal life and furthers his everlasting salvation.

In turn the Protestants agree with the Roman School that fallen man can keep certain precepts of the moral law without the grace of Christ, at least as to the outward work, or absolutely and as to the matter or the doing of the work itself, as the Protestants put it. The Roman School says 'as to the substance of the work'. The two come to the same thing, though some Protestants reject the second way of speaking because the substance of a thing includes both its matter and its form. The question here concerns only the matter of the moral work, not its form, which depends on its end and principle.

source_text: XLVII. Istud videre est apud Davidem Paraeum saepius jam citatum. Fallit igitur, inquit, & fallitur Bellarminus, externum actum operis, & substantiam operis pro eodem sumendo, quae ut pars & totum differunt. Ad substantiam operis requiritur materia & forma, non minus quam ad substantiam hominis requiritur corpus & anima. Actus externus lege praeceptus est pro materia: interna conformitas & mundities, quae habetur ex fide, est pro forma operis, ad quam finis etiam legitimus requiritur. Nam ipse Philosophus non laudat actum virtutis, nisi ex fine, si fiat τοῦ καλοῦ ἕνεκα. Non igitur qui externum operis actum praestat, substantiam operis praestitit. In Bellarm. lib. V. de Gratia & lib. Arbitrio capite 5.
english: Thesis XLVII. This can be seen in David Pareus, already cited so often. 'So Bellarmine deceives and is deceived,' he says, 'when he takes the outward act of a work and the substance of the work to be the same thing, though they differ as part and whole. The substance of a work requires matter and form, no less than the substance of a man requires body and soul.

The outward act the law commands serves as the matter. The inward conformity and purity that comes from faith serves as the form of the work, and a lawful end is also required for it. The Philosopher himself praises an act of virtue only on account of its end, if it is done for the sake of the noble. So whoever performs the outward act of a work has not performed the substance of the work' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 5).

source_text: XLVIII. Verum nullus est apud Protestantes qui non damnet quod quidam in Schola Romana docuerunt, omnia, nempe, & singula legis moralis praecepta, quoad operis substantiam, sive materiam, posse sine Christi gratia servari. Ab hoc enim numero eximunt Protestantes, ut supra vidimus, praecepta quaedam quae spectant actus animi internos, quale est praeceptum de non concupiscendo, & de Deo supra omnia diligendo.
english: Thesis XLVIII. But there is no Protestant who does not condemn what some in the Roman School have taught: that each and every precept of the moral law can be kept without the grace of Christ as to the substance, or matter, of the work.
For, as we saw above, the Protestants except from this certain precepts that concern inward acts of the mind, such as the precept not to covet and the precept to love God above all things.

source_text: XLIX. Praeterea manifestum est ex iis quae diximus, communi Protestantium calculo improbari, quod longe maxima pars Scholae Romanae docet, nimirum praecepta legis moralis faciliora, absque Christi gratia, ab homine corrupto sic observari posse, ut actus sit vere bonus & in eo peccatum vitetur, quanquam ad salutem aeternam non prosit: ac multo magis eorum sententiam qui in ista Schola tenuerunt, totam Naturae legem posse citra gratiam impleri ab homine lapso, aut si non ejus omnia praecepta collective, saltem singula disjunctive, ut in Hispania multi, teste Gabriele Vasquez, sub finem superioris saeculi sentiebant.
english: Thesis XLIX. It is also clear from what we have said that the Protestants by common vote reject what by far the largest part of the Roman School teaches: that the easier precepts of the moral law can be kept by corrupt man without the grace of Christ in such a way that the act is truly good and sin is avoided in it, even though it does nothing for eternal salvation.

Much more do they reject the view of those in that School who held that fallen man can fulfil the whole law of nature without grace, or, if not all its precepts together, at least each one taken singly. Many in Spain thought so toward the end of the last century, as Gabriel Vázquez testifies.

source_text: L. Imo facile ex dictis colligitur, ipsum Gabrielem Vasquez, qui sine gratia Christi nullum opus moraliter bonum perfici posse fatetur, a Protestantibus tamen in eo multum dissentire; quia per gratiam Christi intelligit auxilia quaedam ordinis naturalis, quae infidelibus ipsis, qui tales manent, possunt obtingere. Ac consequenter docet cum plurimis Scholae Romanae Theologis, infideles quoscunque posse, mediantibus auxiliis talibus, opera quaedam vere moraliter bona facere. Protestantes vero per Christi gratiam intelligunt eam solam quae incipit a fide in Christum, eaque viva atque efficaci; ac proinde negant infideles omnes, id est, quicunque non sunt vera fide in Christum imbuti, posse facere ullum opus vere & coram Deo bonum, quodque non habeat peccati rationem, etsi hominum oculis honestum & laudabile videatur.
english: Thesis L. Indeed it follows easily from what has been said that Gabriel Vázquez himself, who admits that no morally good work can be done without the grace of Christ, still differs a great deal from the Protestants here. By the grace of Christ he means certain helps of the natural order that can come even to unbelievers who remain unbelievers. Consequently he teaches, with a great many theologians of the Roman School, that any unbeliever at all can do some truly morally good works by means of such helps.

The Protestants, however, mean by the grace of Christ only the grace that begins with faith in Christ, a faith that is living and effective. So they deny that any unbeliever, that is, anyone not filled with true faith in Christ, can do any work that is truly good and good before God and that lacks the character of sin, however upright and praiseworthy it may look to men.

source_text: LI. Apparet quoque ex iis quae supra retulimus, contrariam sententiam, quae statuit fidem in Christum necessariam non esse, ad hoc ut aliquis bene moraliter operetur, in Ecclesia Romana non ita certam & definitam esse, ut contrarium tenere non liceat; quandoquidem Jansenius, & qui eum sequuntur insignes viri non pauci, idem hac in parte cum Protestantibus aperte docent, nec propterea tamen, ut propter alia multa, publica censura fuit notatus Jansenii liber.
english: Thesis LI. It also appears from what we reported above that the opposite view, which holds that faith in Christ is not necessary for someone to act morally well, is not so certain and defined in the Roman Church that it is forbidden to hold the contrary.

For Jansenius, and a good number of distinguished men who follow him, openly teach the same as the Protestants on this point, and yet Jansenius's book was not publicly censured for this, as it was for many other things.

source_text: LII. Imo non videtur in tota hac quaestione de liberi arbitrii in homine lapso viribus & gratiae necessitate circa bonum morale, ullum esse verum & reale discrimen inter Protestantium & Jansenii doctrinam. Non solum enim cum illis agnoscit Jansenius gratiam Christi, & fidem in eum efficacem & actuosam, necessariam esse ad quodvis opus moraliter bonum, sed etiam, quod consequens est, nullum opus esse vere bonum, quod ex aliquo sincero Dei amore non procedat, & in ejus gloriam non tendat: adeoque frustra apud Scholasticos bona opera distingui, in ea quae pertinent ad pietatem, & salutem aeternam promovent, & ea quae nec ad pietatem spectant, nec prosunt aeternae saluti.
english: Thesis LII. Indeed, in this whole question of the powers of free choice in fallen man and the necessity of grace for moral good, there seems to be no true and real difference between the doctrine of the Protestants and that of Jansenius.

Jansenius acknowledges with them not only that the grace of Christ, and an effective and active faith in him, is necessary for any morally good work. He also holds, as follows from this, that no work is truly good unless it proceeds from some sincere love of God and tends to his glory. And so he holds that the Scholastics distinguish good works to no purpose, into those that belong to godliness and further eternal salvation and those that neither concern godliness nor help toward eternal salvation.

source_text: LIII. Verum est quidem Jansenium nihilominus statuere, cum Concilio Tridentino, opera quaedam bona ab homine fieri posse, priusquam sit justificatus, nec omnia opera quae fiunt ante justificationem esse peccata, & Deo displicere. Cujus contrarium Protestantes videntur communiter asserere, censura sua notantes Canonem Tridentinum, quo anathema dicitur quicunque dixerit, omnia opera quae fiunt ante justificationem, quacunque ratione facta sint, esse peccata.
english: Thesis LIII. It is true that Jansenius nonetheless holds, with the Council of Trent, that a man can do certain good works before he is justified, and that not all the works done before justification are sins and displeasing to God.

The Protestants seem commonly to assert the opposite when they censure the canon of Trent that pronounces anathema on anyone who says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are sins.

source_text: LIV. Sed manifestum est ex iis quae superius exposita fuerunt, Protestantes quum docent, quicquid fit ante justificationem non bonum opus, sed peccatum esse, & cum Augustino dicunt bona opera non praecedere justificandum, sed sequi justificatum, non aliud sibi velle, quam nihil omnino boni fieri posse ante fidem Justificantem, & eos sub justificatione complecti ipsam fidem per quam justificamur: adeoque tum pro eodem habere, bona opera fieri ante justificationem, & fieri ab eo qui adhuc infidelis est. Caeterum, si quis justificationem distinguat ab ipsa fide justificante, & sumat illam praecise pro peccatoris absolutione, & peccatorum ejus remissione, Protestantes eosdem non inficiari quin boni quidam actus, & opera quae Deo placeant, antecedant nostram justificationem. Qualis est in primis ipse actus fidei quae justificat impium, perfugium peccatoris ad Dei misericordiam, dolor de peccatis praeteritis & eorum detestatio, propositum novae vitae, Imploratio divinae gratiae, spes veniae obtinendae & actus alii similes, qui prius natura in homine existant, quam peccata illi remissa sint, & priusquam haberi possit pro justificato.
english: Thesis LIV. But it is clear from what was set out above that when the Protestants teach that whatever is done before justification is sin and not a good work, and say with Augustine that good works do not go before the one who is to be justified but follow the one who is justified, they mean only this: that nothing good at all can be done before justifying faith, and that they include under justification the very faith by which we are justified. For them, then, a good work's being done before justification is the same as its being done by someone who is still an unbeliever.

If, however, someone distinguishes justification from justifying faith itself and takes it precisely for the sinner's absolution and the forgiveness of his sins, the same Protestants do not deny that certain good acts, works that please God, precede our justification.

First among these is the act of the faith that justifies the ungodly, the sinner's flight to God's mercy. Others are sorrow for past sins and hatred of them, the resolve to live a new life, prayer for God's grace, the hope of obtaining pardon, and similar acts. These exist in a man, in the order of nature, before his sins are forgiven and before he can be counted as justified.

source_text: LV. Ex sensu vero Jansenii Synodus Tridentina non definit bona opera fieri ante fidem, sed solum fieri ante justificationem, & anathema non dicit illi qui dixerit opera omnia quae fiunt ante fidem esse peccata, sed tantum illi qui dixerit peccata esse omnia quae fiunt ante justificationem. Nec aliter ipse Bellarminus exponit Canonem Synodi Tridentinae. Neque definit, inquit, Concilium opera infidelium non esse peccata, sed non esse peccata omnia opera, quae justificationem praecedunt. Praecedunt enim justificationem, etiam illa opera quae fiunt a fidelibus, posteaquam in peccatum ceciderunt. Non enim Concilium sequitur regulas Lutheri, qui per omne peccatum mortale voluit fidem amitti: sed regulas Domini, qui Luc. 18. probavit orationem publicani, qui cum fide oravit pro remissione peccatorum. Neque definit idem Concilium, opera fidelium peccatorum absolute non esse peccata, sed addidit, quocunque modo facta. Ut intelligeremus definiri solum a Concilio, quaedam opera fidelium peccatorum non esse peccata, illa videlicet, quae fiunt cum auxilio speciali Dei. De his enim solis proprie Concilium definire voluit, quoniam propositum illi erat agere de justificatione, & iis operibus, quae ad justificationem disponunt: illa vero sola opera ad justificationem disponunt, ut in eodem Concilio habetur, quae initium sumunt a gratia Dei excitante. De Gratia & libero Arbitrio lib. 5. cap. 4. Ex quibus omnibus concludere licet verbalem solum esse contentionem inter Protestantes dum negant, & Jansenium, dum affirmat Bona quaedam opera fieri ante justificationem: imo inter Protestantes, & saepius citatum Canonem Tridentinum, prout illum Jansenius & Bellarminus exponunt.
english: Thesis LV. On Jansenius's reading, the Council of Trent does not define that good works are done before faith, but only before justification. It pronounces anathema not on anyone who says that all works done before faith are sins, but only on anyone who says that everything done before justification is sin. Bellarmine himself explains the canon in just this way.

'The Council does not define,' he says, 'that the works of unbelievers are not sins, but that not all works that precede justification are sins. Even the works done by believers after they have fallen into sin precede justification. For the Council does not follow Luther's rules, who held that faith is lost through every mortal sin, but the Lord's rules, who in Luke 18 approved the prayer of the tax collector, who prayed in faith for the forgiveness of sins.

Nor does the same Council define that the works of sinning believers are not sins without qualification; it added "done in whatever way". So we are to understand that the Council defines only that certain works of sinning believers are not sins, namely those done with God's special help. Only about these did the Council properly mean to define anything, since its purpose was to treat of justification and of the works that dispose to it. And, as the same Council holds, only those works dispose to justification that take their beginning from God's prevenient grace' (On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).

From all this we may conclude that the dispute between the Protestants, who deny, and Jansenius, who affirms, that certain good works are done before justification is only about words. Indeed the same holds between the Protestants and the canon of Trent so often cited, as Jansenius and Bellarmine explain it.

source_text: LVI. Praeterea satis manifestum fecimus, Protestantes docere quidem in statu naturae lapsae, hominem sine gratia esse peccati servum, & veluti captivum: sed illam tamen peccati servitutem, secundum ipsos, non obstare, quominus libere in peccatum feratur, & bonum lege praeceptum aversetur & omittat; ac in eo Arbitrii sui libertatem plene exerceat; cum id faciat non coactus, & ex rationis corruptae deliberato judicio, ac quum hoc aut illud peccatum committit, potestatem habeat ab eo abstinendi.
english: Thesis LVI. We have also shown clearly enough that the Protestants teach that in the state of fallen nature man without grace is the slave of sin and a kind of captive. On their view, though, this bondage to sin does not prevent him from being carried freely into sin, and from turning away from and neglecting the good the law commands.

In this he fully exercises the freedom of his choice, since he acts without compulsion and from the deliberate judgement of a corrupt reason, and when he commits this sin or that one, he has the power to refrain from it.

source_text: LVII. Vidimus quoque illos ultro Scholae Romanae Doctoribus concedere, quod divina gratia, sine qua nihil boni homo agere potest, sic humanam voluntatem movet, ut libertati ejus nihil omnino praejudicet. Quodque bona opera quae per gratiam ab homine fiunt, sunt etiam actus liberi arbitrii non quidem propriis viribus agentis, sed a gratia moti & excitati. Imo Protestantes eosdem non negare quin, posita gratia, homo possit bene & male agere, illosque ipsos qui inter eos sunt rigidiores gratiae assertores, ut qui singulariter Reformati dicuntur, eam quidem efficaciam gratiae tribuere, quae voluntatem ad bonum flectit, & determinat, sed tamen ab ea non tollit omnem aliter agendi facultatem.
english: Thesis LVII. We also saw that they freely grant the doctors of the Roman School that divine grace, without which man can do nothing good, moves the human will in such a way that it does no harm at all to its freedom. Good works done by man through grace are also acts of free choice, acting not by its own powers but moved and roused by grace.

Indeed the same Protestants do not deny that, once grace is given, a man can act well or badly. Even the strictest defenders of grace among them, those called Reformed in a special sense, ascribe to grace an efficacy that bends and determines the will toward good, but still does not take from it every power of acting otherwise.

source_text: LVIII. Adeoque vana est & nulla controversia quam Bellarminus potissimam vocat & esse fingit inter Protestantes omnes ex una parte, & omnes Scholae Romanae Doctores ex altera, nimirum An posito auxilio ad agendum necessario, quodcunque tandem illud sit, homo sit vere proprieque liber in moralibus; sive An posito auxilio gratiae, homo sit vere liberi arbitrii, ita ut praecepta legis violare, vel servare possit. Nec enim quicquam horum Protestantes inficiantur, sed utrumque libenter cum Scholae Romanae Theologis affirmant.
english: Thesis LVIII. So the controversy Bellarmine calls the chief one, and imagines to lie between all the Protestants on one side and all the doctors of the Roman School on the other, is empty and amounts to nothing.

It is whether a man, given the help needed for acting, whatever that help may be, is truly and properly free in moral matters; or whether, given the help of grace, he truly has free choice, so that he can break or keep the precepts of the law. The Protestants deny neither of these; they gladly affirm both with the theologians of the Roman School.

source_text: LIX. Nec repugnat quod saepe apud eos legitur, hominem post peccatum, & ante gratiam, non esse liberi arbitrii, respectu boni moralis. Per hoc enim, ut diximus, nihil aliud significatum volunt, quam voluntatem humanam ante gratiam esse peccati servam, & ex se ad bonum nullas vires habere, quamvis semper in ea maneat libertas illa quae est voluntati essentialis, & quam, fatente ipsa Schola Romana, servitus peccati non tollit, sicut daemonum exemplo evidens est.
english: Thesis LIX. Nor does it conflict with this that we often read in their writers that man after sin and before grace does not have free choice with regard to moral good.

By this, as we have said, they mean only that before grace the human will is the slave of sin and has no strength of its own for good. Yet the freedom essential to the will always remains in it, a freedom which, as the Roman School itself admits, the bondage of sin does not remove, as the example of the demons makes plain.
